notes.key_messages: Candidates should be reminded that throughout this paper they are expected to apply their business knowledge and understanding to an unseen case study or business scenario. This will ensure responses are appropriate for each given situation.  To do well in this paper, candidates must make clear reference, or application, to the accompanying case study. Specific marks are allocated throughout the mark scheme in both parts (a) and (b) for application. In this particular case study, candidates were expected to refer to a company making cars.  Candidates should try to give a full explanation of positive and negative consequences of a business decision when this is asked. Responses require developed reasoning rather than simple description; listed points generally only gain Level 1 whereas an explanation of a point could move the answer to Level 2.  Several questions on this paper ask candidates to make a justified recommendation. Candidates should be reminded that it is important to offer a decision based on balanced argument. The recommendation should compare and make reference as to why the other alternative options were rejected as well as justifying the option that was chosen, without full repetition of the previous analysis.
notes.general_comments: Candidates had generally been well prepared for this examination: It is good to see that many candidates are developing a strong examination technique and clearly understand what is expected of them. The context of SC manufacturing cars provided an accessible scenario for candidates. Those who applied their skills to the context of SC boosted their marks much further. The layout of the examination paper provides side headings in the response areas to prompt candidates in their responses. This seems to work well. Candidates must be reminded to take careful note of how many marks are awarded for each question so they are clear about the extent of developed detail that is required for each answer. The majority of candidates showed good knowledge and understanding of the full range of the syllabus that was assessed, but in a handful of cases it was clear that some topics were not well understood. Candidates should ensure they are prepared to respond to questions on the whole syllabus, as they could earn basic marks by defining business terms and using them confidently. The standard of written English was excellent. Candidates made themselves fully understood and are to be congratulated on the high quality of spelling, punctuation and grammar offered in their responses. There is no penalty for the wrong spelling of words or using incorrect punctuation. Candidates should be reminded to contextualise their responses and not provide generic textbook responses. They must be able to utilise the information provided in the case study and use it in their responses if they are to access the highest marks. For example, in Q4(b) a number of candidates calculated the profitability ratios. Better responses interpreted the results and then gave a clear justification as to whether or not potential shareholders should buy shares in SC by drawing not only on the results of the calculations but also on other information about the business provided in the case study.
notes.1a: The majority of candidates made a good start by correctly identifying two tertiary businesses that SC might use such as a bank for a loan, an advertising agency to produce advertising campaigns, maintenance firms to repair and install the robots and insurance companies to provide cover for their employees or provide customers with insurance. Many responses then went on to explain how the business provided services that SC is likely to use. However, a minority of candidates found it difficult to gain more than one application mark in each section. Application was to answer in the context of a car manufacturer rather than just a generic business and to make reference to the case study especially Appendix 1, such as insurance provided by SC or cars sold through local car showrooms.
notes.1b: Candidates responded well to this question. Most candidates could discuss the effects the three changes had on the company. Many candidates recognised that many customers may want to buy a car using a bank loan and that lower interest rates would make buying a car more affordable with lower interest repayments. Better candidates realised that as SC produced fuel-efficient cars this might actually increase sales for SC rather than cause a reduction in car sales due to people using cheaper substitutes such as motorbikes or public transport. The most common answer to the legal control was that demand for cars would fall as people either used alternative forms of transport or shared cars. A few thought that there would be little effect as people would still want a car even though it could not be used every day. Answers were well applied to the context of buying cars and using alternatives such as public transport. Weaker candidates often just repeated their earlier points in the recommendation and hence gained no further credit or made a weak judgment selecting only one change to justify and gained some additional credit. Strong candidates compared the three changes before making a judgement as to which would have the biggest effect on sales.
notes.2a: This question asked candidates to identify and explain two reasons why employees might want to join a trade union. Many answers discussed the benefits that could be negotiated, such as improved working conditions, more holidays and fewer working hours. The highest credit for this response was, as always, given to candidates who successfully related their explanation to the car company in the case study rather than provide a generic answer. Only strong candidates gained full marks by fully applying their analysis to this business in the case but many did gain application marks in both sections for identifying the problems for the employees at this company as outlined in the case. Weaker candidates often did not explain how the trade union could help improve these issues for workers, such as there being strength in numbers being more effective in pressuring for improvements.
notes.2b: This question was concerned with the effects on SC of three factors when considering the marketing of its cars in foreign markets. Many candidates identified higher levels of competition as being a problem but then only stronger candidates went onto explain how this would affect the marketing in the foreign market. Consumer needs was often the best answered of the factors with candidates arguing that if the car did not meet customer needs then it would not be successful and that market research might be needed before entering the market to ensure customer needs were identified. The channel of distribution attracted weaker responses compared to the other two factors. Weak candidates just stated that a suitable channel needed to be found whilst only really strong candidates considered whether the product needed to be sold through car showrooms where customers could be given information about the product. Some thought selling direct to customers was an option and this often showed a lack of application to the product in the case. Weaker conclusions were usually repetition of earlier statements and hence gained no further credit. Better answers often concluded that consumer needs were the most important of the factors as if customer needs are not met then it does not matter whether the most effective channel of distribution is used, or whether there are no competitors, the cars will not sell. Answers were often well applied through reference to producing cars that meet the exact requirements of customers, choosing car showrooms where customers can come and try the car before buying, reference to the sales figures in Appendix 3 and that SC might be more competitive as it produced fuel-efficient cars.
notes.3a: This question was well answered by the majority of candidates. Candidates often gave answers that recognised making cars to the exact requirements of customers would meet customer needs, encourage brand loyalty and lead to word-of-mouth advertising to family and friends of customers. These answers were often well applied by referring to the cars meeting customer needs but only stronger candidates gained both application marks. Many answers recognised that producing cars to the exact requirements of customers would increase costs and take time to read the bar codes and adjust equipment to make a slightly different car each time. However, most candidates scored less than full marks due to a lack of full application to the case.
notes.3b: This was one of the less well-answered questions on the paper. Many candidates lacked knowledge of the different methods of ensuring quality even if they could name quality control, quality assurance or Total Quality Management. Only a few recognised that SC was already using quality control and if they did they often could not explain how it could be used. There were confused answers that discussed consumers’ test driving the cars and feeding back information to SC. There also seemed to be a lot of confusion between quality control and quality assurance and how they are carried out. Several candidates named quality control and then described quality assurance and vice versa. The majority of candidates did not apply their response to the case study and weak analysis meant solid recommendations were provided by a minority of candidates.
notes.4a: Many candidates gained at least four marks if not more for this question as they could identify methods such as letters, email, text messages, advertising or posters, telephone/mobile phone or noticeboards. The majority of candidates could then go on to explain when these methods might be used, such as telephone to contact suppliers of tyres.
notes.4b: Many candidates scored well by calculating the gross profit, (net) profit and ROCE ratios for both years. Better candidates identified in the recommendation that the business had the same gross profit and (net) profit for both years and had therefore not increased either of these. However, there were lower profitability ratios for all three ratios. Candidates argued that SC is less likely to pay increased dividends in the future and is therefore not worth investing in. Weaker answers just considered what was happening to the figures, e.g. for example revenue increased by $50m or incorrectly calculated the ratios. Few candidates applied their answers to the business in the case and therefore few candidates gained full marks. Where application was awarded it tended to be for identifying the longer term trends in car sales as outlined in Appendix 3 leading to the possibility of increased sales and profit for SC in the future.
